definitions.text: The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly.

The government of the State whose flag the ship is entitled to fly — identical wording to SOLAS's own definition, which the FSS Code cross-references directly rather than restating independently in substance.
The transfer of liquid or gaseous fuel from land-based or floating facilities into a ship's permanent tanks, or the connection of portable tanks to the ship's fuel supply system.

An area in which an explosive gas atmosphere is or may be expected to be present, in quantities requiring special precautions for the construction, installation, and use of equipment. Classified into Zone 0, Zone 1, and Zone 2 based on frequency and duration of explosive atmosphere presence.

A conversion of an existing ship is treated as a 'major conversion' if it substantially alters the ship's dimensions or carrying capacity, changes the ship's type, is intended (in the Administration's view) to substantially prolong the ship's life, or otherwise alters the ship so much that — had it been built new in that form — provisions of MARPOL not applicable to it as an existing ship would now apply. The practical effect is that a major-conversion ship is generally held to new-ship construction/equipment standards rather than the lighter existing-ship standards.

SOLAS does not use the identical defined term, but Chapter II-1 Regulation 1 (Application) reaches the same practical result through different wording: repairs, alterations and modifications 'of a major character' (and outfitting related to them) must meet the requirements for a new ship, so far as the Administration considers reasonable and practicable. Related concept, not an identically-worded definition — flagged here deliberately rather than presented as a matching quote.

definitions.instrument: MARPOL Annex VI (2021 Revised, per MEPC.328(76))
definitions.text: Annex VI defines 'major conversion' using the same four general limbs as Annex I (substantially altering dimensions/carrying capacity/engine power; changing ship type; substantially prolonging the ship's life in the Administration's opinion; or otherwise making the ship subject to new-ship provisions it would not otherwise meet) plus a fifth limb unique to this Annex: a conversion that substantially alters the ship's energy efficiency and includes any modification that could cause the ship to exceed its applicable required EEDI (Reg. 24) or required EEXI (Reg. 25). This fifth limb is the genuinely distinct addition the 2021 revision made to the term.
A rigid survival craft capable of sustaining and protecting occupants during abandonment at sea, complying with LSA Code Section 4.4.

The owner of the ship or any other organization or person such as the manager or bareboat charterer who has assumed responsibility for operation from the owner and agreed to take over all ISM Code duties.
A ship intended primarily to carry dry cargo in bulk, including such types as ore carriers and combination carriers.

term: Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS)

definitions.text: The worldwide integrated radio communications network established under SOLAS Chapter IV, incorporating terrestrial and satellite systems for distress alerting and maritime safety information.
The systematic audit of a Contracting Government by the IMO to verify enforcement of mandatory IMO conventions.

A white light placed over the fore and aft centerline of the vessel showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 225 degrees and so fixed as to show the light from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
The measure of the overall size of a ship determined in accordance with the provisions of Regulation 3 of Annex I of the 1969 Tonnage Convention.
Loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil from the ship, wherever such escape or discharge may occur.

Any discharge into the sea of oil or oily mixture from ships of 400 GT and above is prohibited except when en route, processed through 15 ppm oil filtering equipment, and not originating from cargo pump-room bilges on oil tankers.
A fixed fire-extinguishing installation capable of producing and distributing foam to protect machinery spaces or deck cargo areas.
A group of fire detectors and manual call points served by a single section indicator on the main fire alarm panel.
An inert gas plant and inert gas distribution system designed to maintain an atmosphere in cargo tanks with an oxygen content of not more than 5% by volume.
Any uninsulated surface in an engine room or boiler space having a temperature exceeding 220°C, capable of igniting fuel or oil spray.
Surfaces with temperatures exceeding 220°C which may be impinged as a result of a fuel system failure shall be properly insulated.
A protective suit designed for use by rescue boat crews and marine evacuation system parties which reduces thermal shock upon immersion and provides adequate insulation during rescue operations.

A person who holds a certificate of proficiency in survival craft and rescue boats issued under the authority of, or recognized as valid by, the Administration in accordance with the requirements of the STCW Convention.
The machinery, rudder actuators, steering gear power units and ancillary equipment necessary for applying torque to the rudder stock for steering the ship.

A switchboard which in the event of failure of the main electrical power supply system is directly supplied by the emergency source of electrical power or the transitional source of emergency electrical power and intended to distribute electrical energy to the emergency services.
Machinery spaces provided with automated control, alarm, and fire protection systems approved by the Administration to permit safe operation without continuous engine-room watchkeeping.
Natural gas or other hydrocarbon fuel having a flashpoint below 60°C, carried or used on board ships for propulsion or auxiliary energy generation.
A space containing pumps, compressors and/or vaporizers for fuel preparation and conditioning, provided with dedicated mechanical extraction ventilation maintaining negative pressure.

A machinery space designed to serve as non-hazardous under normal operating conditions, but provided with emergency shutdown arrangements that automatically isolate non-certified electrical equipment and gas supply upon gas detection.

A dedicated space or open deck area on board ship containing bunkering manifolds, isolation valves, emergency release couplings, drip trays, and safety connections for transferring low-flashpoint fuel.

A material which neither burns nor gives off flammable vapours in sufficient quantity for self-ignition when heated to approximately 750°C, as determined by the non-combustibility test specified in Part 1 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.

Divisions formed by bulkheads and decks constructed of steel or equivalent material, stiffened, and insulated with approved non-combustible materials such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (A-60: 60 min, A-30: 30 min, A-15: 15 min, A-0: 0 min), and capable of preventing passage of smoke and flame for 60 minutes.

Divisions formed by bulkheads, decks, ceilings or linings constructed of approved non-combustible materials capable of preventing the passage of flame for 30 minutes, with insulation value such that the average unexposed face temperature rise does not exceed 140°C above original temperature, nor single point 180°C, within the specified time (B-15: 15 min, B-0: 0 min).

The characteristic of a material surface describing its resistance to the propagation of flame under radiant heat exposure, evaluated by measuring Critical Flux at Extinguishment (CFE ≥ 20 kW/m²), Heat for Sustained Burning (Qsb ≥ 1.5 MJ/m²), and Peak Heat Release Rate (qp ≤ 4.0 kW) per Part 5 of Annex 1 to the 2010 FTP Code.
